entries.title: measure S3's bar with nish:simd on mat-vec and both depth documents
entries.body:
* test(self): write S3's two bar kernels with nish:simd and time them as form 5

bench/simd-s3a/mat-vec-simd.ts and depth-simd.ts are the C vector forms'
kernels in nish:simd. bench/simd-s3a.mjs builds them as a fifth column,
refuses either untimed if its IR calls an llvm.x86 or llvm.aarch64
intrinsic, and reports form 5 over form 3, S3's bar.

Refs: docs/wp38-simd.md#s3a-the-bar-kernels-without-a-surface

* docs(self): record S3's bar met by nish:simd on mat-vec and both depth documents

S3a's two kernels written with nish:simd time 1.78x over scalar checked Nish
on mat-vec and 1.62x and 3.81x on the two depth documents, at the median,
against a noise band of 1.00x to 1.03x. They are at C vector's time on
mat-vec and s0 and 8-9% behind it on the sparse log document.

Measured: median 5-over-3 mat-vec 1.78x, s0 1.62x, log 3.81x; copy band 1.00-1.03x; Xeon @ 2.30 GHz, 15 runs
Refs: docs/wp38-simd.md#s3-the-bar-kernels-in-nishsimd-the-bar-met

* docs(self): name the rebased commit the S3 bar was measured at

* docs(self): list mat-vec-simd.ts's Benchmarks Game notice in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: SHA-256 AVX2 message schedule — measured, not built
entries.body:
A C kernel that computes SHA-256's message schedule four words at a time in
AVX2, with the rounds kept scalar, was measured against the Nish body for CPUs
with AVX2 and no SHA-NI. It does not clear the bar of more than 10% outside the
noise band on two runs. On the single 64-byte block an HS256 verify compresses,
it is −5.3% and −9.9% in the baseline build and −1.1% and −0.2% at x86-64-v3,
where LLVM already gives the Nish body rorx and andn. The 64 rounds are one
dependency chain, and that chain sets the time: the kernel runs about 15% fewer
instructions in the same time.

The kernel is kept as bench/sha256-block/avx2.patch, with the numbers, the
reasons it misses and what shipping it would need (it is 3453 bytes of -Oz
.text against the file's 512-byte budget). The runtime is unchanged.
bench/sha256-block/run.mjs gains --avx2 (it refuses a compiler without the
patched kernel), --cpu for every build, --validate, and a CPU stamp.
metrics: 64 B block soft→avx2 −5.3% / −9.9% (bands ±6.2% / ±3.1%) at x86-64, −1.1% / −0.2% at v3; Xeon @ 2.1 GHz (avx2, bmi2, sha_ni, avx512f)
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: take bcrypt's lane bytes as low-and-second-byte pairs
entries.body:
The batched bcrypt kernels (bcryptBody3 to bcryptBody6, behind
bcryptHashN and bcryptCalibrate) now take each lane's four S-box index
bytes as two pairs: a copy of the word behind the value barrier gives
bytes 0 and 1, and that copy moved down by 16 gives bytes 2 and 3. LLVM
reads each pair's second byte with one movzx from ah, bh, ch or dh, so a
lane takes its bytes in six instructions instead of seven. Only four
registers have a second byte, and pairing all six lanes spilled more
than it saved, so the sixth lane of six keeps the previous form. The
one-lane and two-lane kernels are unchanged, as are Secret handling,
wipes, cost and work.

The idea of reading a second byte from a high-byte register is credited
to the multicore-server-challenge's leading kernels: theCatWisel's
rust-epoll-theCatWisel (the challenge's pull request 201),
zig-iouring-nick-potts and asm-epoll-nickita-khylkouski. No code was
copied.

bench/crypto/bcrypt/extract.mjs counts each width's round loop in the
assembly and times the kernels against the previous form and against a
byte-for-byte copy of the module (the noise band).
metrics: Xeon Platinum 8260, cost 10, paired ratio new/old over three runs: 0.962-0.967 at five lanes (21.3 to 20.5 ms a hash), 0.943-0.944 at six, 0.968 at four; noise band 0.995-1.006
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: write the HTTP/1.1 response head with sixteen-byte stores
entries.body:
http1WriteResponseHead now writes "HTTP/1.1 NNN " and the Date, Content-Length
and Connection field names as one 16-byte store of a constant vector each, with
the status digits placed by lane. Each store runs only when the whole head fits
(at + 16 <= at + need <= out.length) and every byte of the head is written after
it, so the extra lanes never survive; otherwise the old byte path runs. Field
values and the date are checked as field text sixteen bytes at a time (the last
vector overlapping the one before), and http1PutText tests the fit once and
copies without a per-byte bounds check. The bytes written, the limits and every
refusal are unchanged; docs/security/http1-codec.md records why.

bench/http1-request drives one keep-alive Http1Connection as Http1Server does,
without sockets: browser (756 B, 251-byte JWT), API-client (338 B, the server's
148-byte HS256 JWT), short, pipelined and split heads, and JsonWriter bodies of
1 to 40 KiB through respond. It reports ns/op against a byte-identical copy and
per-case instruction counts (cachegrind, NISH_SIMD=base, glibc pinned), and its
README ranks the next cuts on this path from per-line callgrind counts.
metrics: 923 instructions fewer a request at x86-64 (996 at v3) on every case — browser −7.0%, api −8.8%, short −19.3%; wall clock repeats outside the copy bands on browser x86-64 (+17.0%, +35.2%), short v3 (+36.6%, +31.8%) and api x86-64 (+13.0%, +9.9%); Xeon @ 2.1 GHz (avx2, bmi2, sha_ni, avx512f), shared cloud host
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: decode base64url four characters a step
entries.body:
base64urlDecode now turns each group of four characters into one 24-bit word
and splits it into three bytes, instead of feeding an accumulator six bits at
a time. It returns the same bytes, or null, as before for every input: the same
refusals of a length of 1 mod 4, of bytes outside the alphabet and of
non-canonical trailing bits. It keeps no branch or table load on the text's
contents. The constant-time assembly check (tests/cases/ct_asm_k1_base64url)
now compiles the shipped group step, so docs/security/crypto-k1.md cites a
check that reads the code that ships.

bench/jwt-verify times an HS256 verify through JwtVerifier and the
hmacCopySha256 midstate verify on the server's real token (header, sub, iat
and exp: a 104-byte signing input, so three compressions), with
NISH_SHA256=soft columns for CPUs without SHA-NI. It also times base64url
decode of each segment against a column in the server's own decoder shape.
metrics: base64url decode −52.4% / −56.2% instructions (148 B / 507 B tokens), −39% to −56% ns across runs; std vs the server's decoder shape 14.5% (run A) and 21.7% (run C) faster at 507 B, no difference at 148 B; Xeon @ 2.1 GHz (avx2, bmi2, sha_ni, avx512f), shared cloud host
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: read Postgres int8 columns with one load and a byte swap
entries.body:
getU64BE in nish/bytes now reads its eight bytes in one guarded step:
off >= 0, off < 2147483640 and off + 8 <= length. LLVM lowers it to one load
and a bswap where the target allows. Any other offset takes the byte loop
unchanged, so every value, panic and panic message is the same as before for
every array and offset. That includes negative offsets, offsets near the i32
maximum, a read ending exactly at the end, one byte short and an empty array.
getI64BE and getF64BE, which binary int8, timestamptz and float8 columns and
int8[] elements decode through, inherit it. The capabilities fixture records
that the first panic site getU64BE reaches is now an index check the guard
rules out; docs/security/bytes.md says why no input gains or loses a panic.

bench/pg-decode replays canned backend bytes through PgConnection's receive
path with no server. It feeds DataRow batches of 1, 20 and 100 with int8, text,
timestamptz, NULL and binary int8[] columns of 0 to 8 elements, framed as the
server's batches are, and the pool and text-format variants. It reports
ns/row against a byte-identical copy and per-case instruction counts
(callgrind, NISH_SIMD=base, glibc pinned). Its README ranks the next cuts on
this path.
metrics: rows 100 151,436 → 120,986 instructions per batch (−20%), pool cases similar; time repeats outside the copy band on pool 20/100 and on rows 20/100 at x86-64-v3, the claim resting on instruction counts; Xeon @ 2.1 GHz (avx2, bmi2, sha_ni, avx512f), shared cloud host
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: store one-byte parts of a join instead of calling memcpy
entries.body:
Array.prototype.join copied every part with llvm.memcpy of a length LLVM could
not see, which lowers to a libc call per part. A part of exactly one byte (what
a byte-at-a-time encoder pushes from String.fromCharCode) is now one load and
one store, and longer or empty parts take the same memcpy as before. The bytes
joined are identical for every part shape: multi-byte UTF-8, empty parts,
separators, and arrays of 0, 1 or many parts. The CG-3 length limit still guards
every path. tests/cases/str_join_byte_parts pins both arms, and
docs/security/codegen.md records the change.

bench/runtime-copies attributes the copies and plain-run scans in this run's
benches and in bench/http1-server.ts, by caller and size. It uses cachegrind
with NISH_SIMD=base and glibc pinned, plus a counting LD_PRELOAD shim
(copycount.c) and a server driver (server.mjs). On the server-shaped program,
libc copies are 1.3-2.2% of a request, spread over five or more small-copy
callers. The largest is the request head that Http1Parser.feed copies into its
own buffer. The bench reproduces the shapes found (small copies, array growth,
checked loops, JSON strings, byte joins), and its README ranks the next cuts.
bench/README.md gains an index of this run's benches.
metrics: chars (a byte-at-a-time join) 3,960 → 3,061 instructions per iteration (−22.7%) and +44.6% ns (band ±8.9%); sha256-block hs256 −3.69% instructions; other programs 0.0% to −0.18%; bench/instructions.json unchanged; Xeon @ 2.1 GHz (avx2, bmi2, sha_ni, avx512f), shared cloud host
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: lowercase and token-check HTTP/1.1 field names sixteen bytes at a time
entries.body:
http1LowerName now checks each field name against RFC 9110's token bytes and
lowercases A-Z sixteen bytes a vector, instead of a byte at a time. The vector
predicate (unsigned lane compares) refuses exactly what http1IsTokenByte
refuses: controls, SP, HTAB, DEL, bytes 0x80 and above, and the 17 delimiters.
Only A-Z changes case. The vector runs only while sixteen bytes fit in the held
head, masks the lanes past the name, and leaves the tail to the old byte loop,
so it reads and writes nothing past the name or the buffer. Every accept,
reject, status and stored name and value is unchanged.
net_http1_parse_diff now drives 237,143 heads, with every delimiter at every
position, against a frozen copy of the old parser.

The OWS scan after the name is bounded by buf.length directly. The checker had
lost that fact after the new call and kept a bounds check (NL9007), which the
performance gate caught. The scan's result is the same.
metrics: browser request −781 instructions at x86-64 (−6.8%) and −1,028 at x86-64-v3 (−8.1%); api −544 / −712; wall clock repeats outside both copy bands on api at x86-64 (+11.3%, +22.2%); Xeon @ 2.1 GHz (avx2, bmi2, sha_ni, avx512f), shared cloud host
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: box fresh array fields of unknown length as { len, data }
entries.body:
* perf(codegen): box fresh array fields of unknown length as { len, data }

Experimental. A class array field that the inline rule admits but whose
assigned lengths are not all constants (or are too long for the slots)
keeps only its len and data in the object, a 16-byte slice as Rust's
Box<[T]> does: no separate 24-byte header, one allocation fewer per
object, and one dependent load fewer per element access.

* docs(codegen): document boxed array fields and add their tests

LANGUAGE.md and ARCHITECTURE.md describe the boxed layout, its aliasing
argument and when a field falls back to it; cls_boxed_array covers every
fresh right-hand side, cls_boxed_array_push the negative.

Tests: tests/cases/cls_boxed_array, tests/cases/cls_boxed_array_push

* test(codegen): regenerate goldens for boxed array fields

* test(self): regenerate checked goldens for boxed array fields

* fix(codegen): name the boxed field's debug type apart and test both boxing reasons

The DWARF composite of a boxed field is now `<T[]> slice`, so a debugger
cannot take it for the array header of the same element type. Adds a
boxed field over the 256-byte inline cap to cls_boxed_array and a CG-1/CG-2
link test for `new Array` through a boxed field, and corrects the docs on
when a field is boxed and on who shares the header's TBAA scalars.

Tests: tests/cases/cls_boxed_array, tests/link/cg_sec_boxed_new_array

* test(codegen): regenerate goldens for boxed fields across modules

JsonTokenizer's stack is now a boxed field, so the std_json_typed link
goldens move with it. cg_sec_boxed_new_array imports its class from a
second module, as every link program must.

* fix(codegen): keep FieldInfo unpadded and the boxed literal loop proven

FieldInfo's boxed flag sits with the other booleans so the record stays 72
bytes, and the boxed literal's store loop bounds itself on values.length so
the performance ratchet sees no new bounds check. One Http3Server slot is
1,152 bytes smaller now that its unknown-length array fields are boxed.

* test(self): regenerate checked goldens for the FieldInfo reorder

* fix(codegen): keep the boxed field paths clear of new ratchet warnings

The debug-info branch for boxed and inline array fields now looks up the
element type and its name once, and the boxed literal store loop walks its
values with for-of, so neither adds an NL9011 or NL9007 past the baseline.

* docs(codegen): regenerate the IR cookbook and self goldens for boxed fields

The arr-repeat-check entry's Perm now stores its array as { i64, i8* }.

entries.title: write Postgres integer parameters' digits once, two a step
entries.body:
* perf(net): write putDecimal's digits once, two a step, into their places

Work in progress: measurements, goldens and docs follow.

* docs(net): record pgPutDecimal's scope and panic site

* perf(net): write Postgres integer parameters' digits once, two a step

paramInt, paramIntArray and arrayInt write each i64 through putDecimal,
which wrote a digit at a time with a signed % and / and a checked store,
then reversed the digits. It now reserves pgDecimalLength(value) bytes and
pgPutDecimal fills them once, right to left, two digits a step from a
200-byte table, on the magnitude as a u64. One guard proves the window, so
the stores carry no per-digit bounds check. The bytes on the wire are the
same for every i64; tests/link/std_postgres_decimal checks them against the
old writer, and with a number ending at the output buffer's last byte.

The bench README records the result and re-ranks what is left:
arrayElement first, then the rest of putDecimal.

Measured: params 100 138,193 instr/op against base 149,900 (+8.5%) at x86-64, 138,193 against 148,846 (+7.7%) at x86-64-v3; params 20 +6.7% / +6.0%; every rows, text and pool case 53 instr/op lower
Measured: ns/op base vs nish, two runs each, outside the copy band both times: params 100 +17.4% (±1.9%) and +20.8% (±4.0%) at x86-64; params 20 +9.6% (±2.3%) and +13.5% (±1.0%), params 100 +15.8% (±13.1%) and +11.9% (±1.7%) at x86-64-v3; params 1 is noise
Refs: bench/pg-decode/README.md
Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_decimal

* docs(net): say how the putDecimal cut takes its two digits

The bench README said a 200-byte table; the writer divides the u64 magnitude by 100 and splits each pair, with no table.

* test(net): name the i64 limits in the decimal test, and check the bytes past it

Answers review on the putDecimal cut. The decimal test names the i64 limits
instead of indexing into its value list, and adds three cases that end the
number three bytes short of the output buffer's end and check those bytes
are untouched. The bench README and the security record say the reservation
is now the number's length rather than 20 bytes, so the buffer may grow one
call later while the wire bytes stay the same; the README also says the time
gains are about twice the instruction gains, that params 20 at x86-64 did
not repeat, and that rank 2's per-call count covers a different region than
the per-integer saving.

Tests: tests/link/std_postgres_decimal

* test(self): regenerate the jwt-verify and pg-decode goldens for boxed array fields

#1189 boxes fresh array fields of unknown length as { len, data }, which moves
struct sizes and field offsets. The checked goldens for bench/jwt-verify (stale
on main since #1189 landed) and bench/pg-decode still recorded the old layout.
Regenerated with node tests/self/goldens.js --update; no other golden moved.
